sentences.text: If an AI writes the code today, who pays for it when somebody has to change it next year?
One research team stopped guessing and ran a randomised trial: code written with or without AI, then changed by hand.
The worry has a familiar shape: one study collected in a review of the research warns that code built up through conversation often "lacks cohesive structure", which makes later maintenance harder.
And on security, the Razorwire Cybersecurity channel put it bluntly: "46% of AI generated code is reportedly uh contain some form of security weakness".
So what happened in that trial when people had to change code an AI had helped write?
On speed, nothing reliable: their completion times were consistent with no effect at all.
The authors are careful about what that means: any difference was at most small, and highly uncertain, which is not the same as proof there is none.
On quality, the code's health score after the changes showed no reliable difference either, and test coverage was essentially identical.
A second, Bayesian analysis even hinted at a small gain in code health when the original was written with AI by someone who uses it habitually.
Dave Farley, talking about the study, summed it up: "The AI didn't make it any better and it didn't make it any worse."
So where does the debt fear get its evidence?
Partly from surveys: one study measured maintainability and technical debt through its respondents' answers to questionnaire scales, and AI use went with lower maintainability and more debt.
That is an association in people's answers, not a timed test of someone else changing the code.
The review of the research counted the worry too: maintainability concerns came up in 11 of its sources, 23 percent.
That counts how often the concern is raised, which is not the same as measuring it.
Then there is code out in the wild: a study that tracked commits made with AI coding assistants found that some of the issues they introduced still survive in the latest code.
The assistants fixed about as many code smells, surface problems like naming and formatting, as they introduced; but they introduced more correctness and security issues than they fixed.
But the authors did not compare those commits with code written by people alone, so the study cannot say AI code leaves more debt than human code does.
And the security worry? One study did put a number on it: of 733 code snippets generated by AI, 27.3 percent contained security weaknesses.
That is a count of weaknesses in AI code alone; it cannot tell you whether code written by hand would score any better on the same check.
The review of the research found security risk was the challenge its sources raised most, in 10 of them, half of those it tallied for that question.
What those sources agree on is narrower than a rate: generated code may contain weaknesses when developers rely on it without rigorous checking.
There is one cost, though, that experiments did measure, and it lands on the person who wrote the code.

In one trial, crowd workers recruited online, most of them freelance or professional software developers, did a coding task with or without AI, then took a quiz on the skills the task should have built.
Using AI did not make them significantly faster, and their scores came out lower by a gap worth 17 percent of the quiz.
In a separate experiment with different participants, working with AI cut their chance of answering questions about their own code correctly by 5.95 percentage points.
The authors re-checked it other ways: each time the drop kept its direction, though in one it was too weak to be sure of.

So, is AI-written code harder to maintain? In the one trial that tested it, over the time it ran, no: no reliable difference in speed or code health, though one trial with that much uncertainty cannot rule out a small one.
The louder warnings rest on questionnaires, counts of concern and issue tallies with nothing human to compare them to.

The cost that was measured is different: in both of those experiments, people working with AI learned less or understood their own code less well, and whether that makes it harder for those same people to change their code later is something none of these studies tested.
Simon Willison draws his line here: "I don't think you should ever commit a line of code that a language model wrote If you don't understand it yourself".
So when you review AI-assisted code, yours or a colleague's, don't stop at whether it works: ask the author to walk you through it with the AI closed.
If they can't, the code isn't finished yet.
